zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0. Supplied index: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription and explanatory notes are this reviewer's scan-based work; the index is an identification aid, not diplomatic authority.

lines.note: Inyen is a principle or cause. The scan reads Principio, not Pencipio, and refers the reader to Innen with doubled n; this entry is anticipated by the preceding page's catchword.
This separate Inyen is equated with sakamori, a drinking gathering or entertainment. Beberetes distinguishes it from the preceding causal term.

runs.text: Palaura de liuros que ſe toma por noi-

lines.note: Inyo is introduced as a bookish term covering complementary opposites. Noi- begins noite, the first member of the night-and-day pair on the next row.

runs.text: te, & dia, ceo, & terra, molher, & homẽ,

lines.note: Completes night and day, followed by heaven and earth, woman and man. These are the dictionary's illustrative pairs for inyo, not separate headwords.
Inyo qeookwai names a conjunction or union. The caron in Inyǒ and circumflex in qeôquai are distinct printed marks; the Portuguese specifies the partners below.
The first conjunction is that of man and woman. Item then opens a broader explanation, with Ajunta- continued on the next physical row.

runs.text: mento de couſa como materia, & forma de q̃

lines.note: Completes ajuntamento and uses matter and form as a philosophical analogy. The singular couſa and the abbreviated q̃ are retained as printed rather than regularized.
Matter and form are said to compose perceptible things. Inyǒ begins the next Japanese expression, completed by zuijun on the following row.
Zuijun completes the inyo expression, glossed as the composition or combination of these two principles. The demonstrative destas refers forward to duas couſas below.

The two principles are explicitly named In and yǒ within the Portuguese explanation. Lowercase italic ſ. introduces the specification here; it is not the upright capital S usage label. The gloss starts another matter-and-form analogy.
Completes matter and form and adds moisture and heat as another explanatory pair. The historical spellings humidade and quentura are retained.
Inyoku is defined as carnal desire. The phrase 'desires of the flesh' is divided after da and completed in the next short row.
Carne completes the desire-of-the-flesh definition. Its r-n sequence was misread as m in the draft's came; the entire word is printed in italic.
Inyu is another term identified with innen and glossed as a principle or cause. The doubled n in Innen agrees with the cross-reference at the top of the page.

Inzan means visiting the court of the retired sovereign. The Japanese paraphrase has doubled n and the visible spelling Innogoxeye, rather than the draft's Inogoxoye; the Portuguese identifies the sovereign below.

runs.text: Rey que ja renunciou o gouerno.

lines.note: The king in question has already relinquished government. This completes the definition of attendance on a retired sovereign, rather than an ordinary royal audience.
Inzot means taking someone along in company. The final t is retained as part of the historical spelling, and the final upright S marks written usage.

Ippa is explained as one religious group or sect. The section-opening I is an enlarged initial spanning this and the next row; the following capital P belongs to the same headword and was not an italic standalone letter.
Seita completes the definition as a sect. The left-hand stroke in this crop is the lower part of the preceding line's enlarged I, not another character to add to this row.
This separate Ippa means one wave, explicitly paraphrased by hitotsu no nami. The upright S is the written-usage label.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de encher de todo, ou

lines.note: Ippai is introduced as an adverb describing complete filling or fullness. The alternative state, being full, continues below.
Choodo ippai iruru illustrates filling something right up. En- is wholly italic Portuguese and begins encher, not a mixed roman-and-italic Japanese fragment.

runs.text: cher de todo botando em algũa vaſilha. ¶

lines.note: Completes encher and explains filling a container completely. I- starts Igrejani in the next example; the line's algũa keeps its observed tilde carrier.
Completes the example that people have come to fill the church. The Portuguese prints Eſtaa with doubled a before the separate article a; this historical form is not shortened to the draft's Eſta.

runs.text: ja chea, & abarrotada de gente que veo.

lines.note: Completes Igreja and describes the church as full and crowded with those who came. The historical singular veo follows the collective gente as printed.
The figurative extension of ippai concerns drawing a bow fully before releasing an arrow. Fa- begins hanatsu on the next row; fijte is retained in the printed historical spelling.

runs.text: Tirar com frecha embebendõ o ar-

lines.note: Completes hanatsu, to release or shoot. The Portuguese explains shooting an arrow with the bow fully drawn; the tilde in embebendõ is retained and ar- begins arco below.
Completes arco todo, specifying the full draw of the bow. This short continuation closes the example rather than starting a new sense.
Ippan is one bowl of rice. Goqui names the bowl within the Portuguese definition and is printed in italic here; the initial I of the headword replaces the draft's lowercase l.
The second Ippan means one sail, as hitotsu no ho makes explicit. The maritime qualification is divided after ma-.
Rear completes marear, identifying a sailing sail rather than a candle. The upright S is the written-usage label.

runs.text: Hum bule, ou pichel de vinho.

lines.note: Ippei is a vessel's measure of wine or sake, described as a pot or pitcher. The gloss's two vessel names are Portuguese alternatives, not separate Japanese forms.
Ippen or ippenni means wholeheartedly or exclusively. Soo continues into mente below; the absence of a visible hyphen is retained.
Completes somente and gives an example of single-mindedly desiring the next-life goal. The Portuguese renders this as desiring salvation, beginning with De-; the tilded ippẽni is not expanded.

runs.text: ſejar de coração, & ſem miſtura de outra cou

lines.note: Completes desejar and emphasizes heartfelt desire unmixed with anything else. Cou continues into couſa on the next row without an added hyphen.
Completes couſa and supplies salvation as the object of desire. This closes the religious example of wholehearted aspiration.
The Japanese hisago identifies a gourd, but the Portuguese visibly reads cabeça rather than the expected cabaça. This apparent printed anomaly is retained. The final upright S marks written usage.
Ippyoshi denotes one tone or beat. The initial is capital I, not long s; the Japanese example starts with Ip-, outside the italic Portuguese gloss.
Completes ippyooshi ni odoru, dancing to a single rhythm or beat. Hũ begins the phrase specifying one and the same rhythm below.
Completes the explanation as dancing in the same tone or measure. The source's single-s spelling compaſo is retained.
Ippit is explained by hitofude and glossed as a letter, then as a short piece of writing. The missing initial I is restored from the scan; the final t remains unexpanded.
The second sense is a written note or brief letter. This completes the preceding Itẽ phrase.
Ippo means one law or rule, as hitotsu no nori explains. The caron in the headword is retained distinctly from the circumflexes in Ippiô and Ippiôxi.
Ippon names a particular rank or dignity. The gloss itself does not further specify the institution or rank system; no more specific identification is inserted into the transcription.
Ippuku literally names one belly or womb. The example continues at the top of the next column, where it describes siblings of the same womb.
Continues the example after ippuku, one womb: siblings born of the same womb. The headword fragment is Ippucu with two p types, and the Portuguese adjective is meſmo, not the OCR meſino.
Completes the description of siblings of the same womb. This belongs to the preceding column's Ippucu entry, not to a separate sense of the next headword.

Ippuryu describes something singular or out of the ordinary. The final vowel carries a caron; the draft's rifi-like ending is damaged-letter recognition rather than a different Japanese form. The supplied NINJAL entry 132d01 subsequently corroborates the headword identification.

Finishes the definition as different from the common run, then gives ippuryu na hito, an exceptional person. Differente is visible; the apparent extra I before the example is not a separate printed letter.
Translates the example as a person singular or extraordinary in some respect. The tilded contraction nalgũa is retained rather than expanded.
Supplies the unspecified respect in which the person is exceptional. It completes the example's Portuguese translation.

Ike is a pond or tank of water. The large initial I belongs to this headword and spans two physical rows; the following Q is also capital. The crop includes the full initial rather than assigning its lower part to the next entry.
A distinct homonymous ike means the house of a physician. The small upright initial is I, not long s; the enlarged I to its left belongs to the preceding pond entry.
The verb means to cause to live or keep alive, with the printed principal forms ike, ikuru, iketa. Toriuo begins the example about preserving a bird's life.
Completes the example: keep a bird alive without killing it. Paßa- begins Portuguese passaro with the source's double-s ligature.
Completes the bird's gloss and starts a further example about saving a person's life. The final iqu- continues on the next row.
Finishes ikuru and translates it as saving someone's life. Fiuo starts the fire-preservation example, not another person's-life phrase.

runs.text: Permet. Cobrir o fogo com cinza

lines.note: Hi wo ikuru is explained metaphorically as covering a fire with ashes. The verb remains roman while the explanatory instruction is italic.
Completes the reason for banking the fire: so that it lasts. Hana wo ikuru begins a new example about keeping flowers fresh, whose explanation starts with putting their stems in water.

runs.text: pees das roſas, ou flores na agoa pera que eſ-

lines.note: The gloss specifies the bases or stems of roses or other flowers in water. Eſ- continues into eſtejão below; pees is retained as the printed historical spelling.

Completes the flower-freshness explanation and begins an example about preserving chestnuts, mandarins, and similar produce. The visible tilde in micã represents the nasal ending missing from the OCR mica; no hyphen is supplied after iqu.
Finishes the fruit-preservation verb. The Portuguese names chestnuts, oranges, and other fruit, a broader rendering of the Japanese examples rather than a separate entry.

runs.text: fruita de baixo da terra, area, &c. pera que

lines.note: Explains storage beneath earth or sand to preserve the fruit. The separated de baixo and historical area are retained without modernization.
Completes the purpose clause: so that the stored fruit lasts. This closes the long entry on causing or allowing things to remain alive or fresh.
Ikedoru means to capture alive, specifically in war in the following continuation. The headword gives verbal principal forms rather than only the noun for a live capture.
Completes the wartime setting and begins equivalent expressions for taking a person alive. The second construction continues as ikedori ni suru below.
Completes ikedori ni suru, making someone a live captive. Idem identifies it as equivalent to the preceding verbal expression, not a new definition.
Ikemizu is water from a pond or tank. The printed doubled zz is retained rather than normalized to a modern romanization.
Iki is breath. Iki wo tsuku begins a collocation explained as breathing out, with the force of the exhalation specified on the next row.
Completes the forceful-exhalation gloss and starts iki wo tomuru, holding one's breath. The division tomu-/ru is kept at the physical line ending.
Finishes holding the breath and introduces expressions for the breath ceasing. The lowercase l introduces tayuru as an alternative continuation below.
Iki ga tayuru is paired with iki ga kiruru: to stop breathing or die. The scan's nasal-mark placement in Naõ and the ordinary f in resfolegar are retained.
Jinba ni iki wo tsugasuru means allowing men and horses to catch their breath. The line-final tilded descã- begins the Portuguese word for resting.
Completes the explicit reference to men and horses, confirming the reading jinba. A new breath-related collocation begins with Iqiuo at the end.
Iki wo yasumuru is to rest. The following iki wo tsukikakuru begins here and runs into the next row, where an alternative verb is supplied.
Completes tsukikakuru and gives shikakuru as an alternative: breathing or blowing upon something. The Portuguese al- continues into algũa below.
Finishes the object of breathing upon something and introduces iki ga kayo, the breath passing to and fro. Its Portuguese explanation continues with inhalation and exhalation.
Clarifies breathing as the breath entering and leaving. Iki ga faz-/zumu starts the next expression, whose doubled z is preserved across the physical division.

Completes iki ga hazzumu, here glossed as breathing with difficulty. The Portuguese word is Resfolegar with f, not the OCR Resſolegar; this is a meaningful letter correction supported by the printed cross-stroke and context.
Iki wo tsugu is to catch one's breath while resting. The narrow space in Res folegar is retained rather than silently joining the source's provisional spacing.
This homonymous verb means to go; the dictionary recommends yuki/yuku as the better form. Meliùs and Vt belong to the italic editorial apparatus, while the alternative Japanese form is roman.
The example is going to Arima, with iku and yuku offered as alternatives. It is wholly Japanese text, not a Portuguese sentence with an embedded term.
A separate verb means to live or be alive, with ikuru as the printed nonpast form. Ino- starts inochi, life, in the following example.
Completes inochi wo ikuru and marks it as having the same meaning, living one's life. The initial fragment belongs to inochi rather than a separate headword.
Ikiai, with its printed inflected forms, means meeting someone on the road. The carons in the principal forms are retained without changing the historical conjugation.
Supplies the person encountered and closes the preceding verbal definition. This is not part of the following horse-remedy entry.

runs.text: Mezinha que ſe dà ao caualo cãnſado

lines.note: This homonymous ikiai is a remedy given to a tired horse. The scan visibly carries a tilde over the a of cãnſado even though an n is also printed; that redundant-looking mark is retained, not normalized away.
States the remedy's purpose: to restore the horse's breath or vigor. The gloss gives a use, not the ingredients of the treatment.

runs.text: Filhos de duas peßoas, as quaes por

lines.note: Ikiai kyodai denotes children brought into a sibling relation by their parents' marriage. The headword ends in i; peßoas has the double-s ligature, and quaes replaces garbled OCR. The explanation continues across the page turn. NINJAL 132d12 records a caron in qiǒdai, but no secure corresponding mark is visible here, so this impression remains qiodai.

runs.text: ſe caſarem ambas ficão os filhos como dous ir-

lines.note: Explains that when the two parents marry, their children become like two siblings. Filhos restores the clearly printed l missing from the OCR. The final ir- continues as mãos on the next page; the repeated bottom mãos is a catchword, not an additional body line.
